key_terms.meaning: An ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits a continuous spectrum depending only on its temperature T
The smallest packet of energy, E = hν, where ν is frequency in hertz and h is Planck's constant
h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, the fixed step size between allowed energy values
The wrong prediction of classical physics that a black body radiates infinite energy at short wavelengths
A single quantum of light carrying energy E = hν and momentum p = h/λ
φ, the minimum energy in joules needed to free an electron from a metal surface
ν₀ = φ/h, the lowest light frequency that can eject electrons from a given metal
Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ), the increase in X-ray wavelength after scattering through angle θ
λ = h/p, the matter-wave wavelength of a particle of momentum p
The rule that matter and radiation each show wave behaviour in one experiment and particle behaviour in another
Electrons fired at a nickel crystal form diffraction maxima, proving electrons behave as waves
v_p = ω/k, the speed at which one crest of the matter wave travels; it is not the particle speed
v_g = dω/dk, the speed of the wave packet, which equals the classical particle velocity
Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2: position and momentum cannot both be measured with unlimited sharpness
ψ(x,t), a complex-valued amplitude that completely describes the state of a quantum particle
|ψ|², whose value at a point times dx gives the chance of finding the particle between x and x + dx
A state of definite energy whose probability density |ψ|² does not change with time
−(ℏ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² + V(x)ψ = Eψ, the equation for states of definite energy E
A particle trapped between walls where V = ∞; its energies are Eₙ = n²h²/(8mL²), n = 1, 2, 3…
A particle crossing a barrier even when its energy E is less than the barrier height V₀

takeaways: Planck saved the black-body spectrum only by allowing energy exchange in steps of hν, and that single assumption started quantum physics.
One photon ejects one electron with maximum kinetic energy hν − φ, which explains why brighter light gives more electrons but not faster ones.
Compton scattering shows a photon carrying momentum h/λ, so light must be treated as a particle in collisions.
Every moving body has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, which is measurable for electrons but unmeasurably small for a cricket ball.
The Davisson-Germer diffraction pattern of electrons turned matter waves from an idea into an experiment.
The wave packet travels at the group velocity, which equals the particle velocity; the phase velocity of a matter wave is not the particle speed.
The uncertainty principle is a limit set by nature, not by the clumsiness of instruments.
The wavefunction is not directly measurable; only |ψ|² has physical meaning, and it must be normalised.
The Schrodinger equation plays the same role for matter that Newton's second law plays for classical particles.
Trapping a particle between rigid walls allows only certain energies, so confinement itself causes quantisation.
Tunnelling probability falls exponentially with barrier width and height, which powers the scanning tunnelling microscope and limits shrinking transistors.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always want a clean derivation, the boundary conditions written down explicitly, the physical meaning of the final result, and a labelled sketch of ψ or |ψ|².

bank.q: State Planck's hypothesis. Explain how it removes the ultraviolet catastrophe and fits the observed black-body spectrum.
outline: Classical Rayleigh-Jeans law predicts intensity rising as 1/λ⁴ and infinite total energy
Wien's law fits short wavelengths only; both fail somewhere
Planck's assumption: oscillators emit or absorb energy only in multiples of hν
Average energy per oscillator becomes hν/(e^(hν/kT) − 1) instead of kT
Resulting curve peaks and falls; matches experiment at all wavelengths
Wien displacement λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K appears as a consequence

bank.q: Explain the photoelectric effect and Einstein's photoelectric equation. Use it to explain the effect of intensity and frequency on the emitted electrons.
outline: Define work function φ and threshold frequency ν₀ = φ/h
Einstein's equation: hν = φ + ½mv²_max
Stopping potential eV₀ = hν − φ and its use in finding φ
Intensity controls number of photons and hence photocurrent, not maximum energy
Frequency controls maximum kinetic energy; below ν₀ no emission at any intensity
Emission is instantaneous because one photon gives all its energy to one electron

bank.q: What is the Compton effect? Derive the expression for the Compton shift and state its significance.
outline: X-ray photon of energy hν collides with a loosely bound electron at rest
Conservation of energy: hν + mₑc² = hν′ + √(p²c² + mₑ²c⁴)
Conservation of momentum in two perpendicular directions
Eliminate electron momentum to get Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ)
Compton wavelength h/mₑc = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m
Significance: photon has momentum h/λ, so light behaves as a particle in collisions
The unshifted line comes from tightly bound electrons of the whole atom

bank.q: State the de Broglie hypothesis and describe the Davisson-Germer experiment that confirmed it.
outline: λ = h/p; for kinetic energy K, λ = h/√(2mK)
For an electron accelerated through V volts, λ = 12.27/√V angstrom
Apparatus: electron gun, nickel target, movable detector, vacuum
Nickel crystal acts as a grating with known spacing
Diffraction maxima at particular angles, matching Bragg's law
Measured wavelength agrees with h/p, confirming matter waves
Wave nature is not visible for heavy bodies because λ is tiny

bank.q: Derive the energy eigenvalues and normalised wavefunctions for a particle in a one-dimensional infinite potential well.
outline: Set V = 0 inside 0 < x < L and V = ∞ outside
Write the time-independent Schrodinger equation and solve: ψ = A sin kx + B cos kx
Boundary condition ψ(0) = 0 gives B = 0
Boundary condition ψ(L) = 0 gives kL = nπ, so k = nπ/L
Eₙ = n²h²/(8mL²), n = 1, 2, 3…
Normalise to get A = √(2/L)
Show that n = 0 is not allowed and that energy is never zero; spacing grows with n

bank.q: Obtain the transmission probability for a particle of energy E tunnelling through a rectangular barrier of height V₀ and width a, when E < V₀. Discuss the result.
outline: Three regions; oscillatory solutions outside, decaying exponential inside the barrier
Match ψ and dψ/dx at both boundaries
Transmission T ≈ 16 (E/V₀)(1 − E/V₀) e^(−2αa) with α = √(2m(V₀ − E))/ℏ
T falls exponentially with width a and with √(V₀ − E)
T is not zero even for wide barriers, so classical reflection is not complete
Comment on sensitivity: a small change in a changes T a lot

bank.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, the stopping potential and the threshold wavelength.
outline: Photon energy E = hc/λ = 3.1 eV (use hc = 1240 eV·nm)
K_max = E − φ = 1.1 eV
Stopping potential V₀ = 1.1 V
Threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc/φ = 620 nm
State clearly that intensity would not change these values

bank.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V and compare it with that of an electron at 10 keV and of a 1 g object moving at 10 m/s.
outline: λ = h/√(2meV) = 12.27/√V angstrom
At 100 V, λ ≈ 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, comparable to atomic spacing
At 10 keV, λ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m, so the electron probes smaller distances
For the 1 g object, λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m, far too small to detect
Conclude why diffraction is seen for electrons but not for everyday objects

bank.q: Using the uncertainty principle, estimate the minimum kinetic energy of an electron confined to a region of size equal to a typical nucleus (10⁻¹⁴ m) and comment on the result.
outline: Take Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁴ m and Δp ≥ ℏ/(2Δx)
Δp ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻²¹ kg·m/s
K ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 1 MeV or more
Compare with a few MeV of nuclear binding energy
Conclude that an electron cannot be held inside a nucleus

bank.q: Distinguish between phase velocity and group velocity for a matter wave. Show that the group velocity equals the particle velocity and that v_p v_g = c² for a relativistic particle.
outline: Definitions v_p = ω/k and v_g = dω/dk
A particle is a wave packet, a superposition of many k values
Compute ω from E = ℏω and p = ℏk, giving v_p = E/p
Differentiate to get v_g = dE/dp = p/m = particle velocity
For relativistic case v_g = v and v_p = c²/v, so v_p v_g = c²
Phase velocity carries no energy or information; only the packet does

bank.q: Explain the Born interpretation of the wavefunction. List the conditions ψ must satisfy and why normalisation is necessary.
outline: ψ is a complex amplitude with no direct physical meaning
|ψ|² dx is the probability of finding the particle between x and x + dx
ψ must be single-valued, continuous, with continuous first derivative where V is finite
ψ must vanish at infinite potential walls and be finite everywhere
Normalisation ∫|ψ|² dx = 1 fixes the scale factor
Superposition and the measurement of an average value follow from this interpretation

bank.q: Explain quantum tunnelling and its applications. Why is tunnelling more likely for light particles and thin barriers?
outline: Physics of the barrier region: exponentially decaying wavefunction
T depends on e^(−2αa); α grows with particle mass and barrier height
Electrons tunnel easily, protons much less, macroscopic bodies never
Applications: scanning tunnelling microscope, tunnel diode, Josephson junction, alpha decay, flash memory
STM resolution comes from the steep exponential dependence on gap width
Limitation: tunnelling leakage in very thin gate oxides of small transistors

bank.q: Trace how black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect and the Compton effect together forced the collapse of classical physics and the birth of quantum mechanics.
outline: Classical wave theory: energy is continuous, and Maxwell's equations allow any amplitude
Black-body spectrum could not be fitted; Planck needed energy quanta hν
Photoelectric effect contradicted wave ideas: threshold frequency and instantaneous emission
Einstein extended the quantum idea to light itself and explained the threshold
Compton scattering provided momentum evidence: photon momentum h/λ
Common thread: energy and momentum are exchanged in discrete packets
Contrast with Newtonian determinism and continuous energy of classical mechanics

bank.q: Extend the one-dimensional infinite well to a three-dimensional cubical box of side L, obtain the energy eigenvalues, and discuss degeneracy.
outline: Separate variables: ψ = X(x)Y(y)Z(z)
Each direction gives a one-dimensional box problem with the same boundary conditions
E = (h²/8mL²)(n_x² + n_y² + n_z²)
Each state labelled by three quantum numbers, all positive integers
Lowest state (1,1,1) is non-degenerate
States like (1,1,2), (1,2,1), (2,1,1) have the same energy: degeneracy
Note how box size L shrinks the level spacing as the box grows

glossary.def: Taking in of radiation by a body, which for a black body is complete at every wavelength.
The distribution of radiation given out by a body as a function of wavelength or frequency.
The wavelength of peak emission falls as temperature rises, λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K.
The reverse voltage just large enough to stop the fastest photoelectrons, giving their maximum kinetic energy as eV₀.
The current produced by photoelectrons in a photocell; its size depends on how many electrons are emitted per second.
hν = φ + ½mv²_max, the energy balance for one photon ejecting one electron.
The constant h/mₑc = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m that sets the size of the wavelength shift in Compton scattering.
The electron set in motion in a Compton collision, which carries the lost energy and momentum.
The wave associated with a moving particle, with wavelength λ = h/p and frequency ν = E/h.
A group of waves of slightly different wavelengths that adds up to a localised pulse representing a particle.
nλ = 2d sin θ, the condition for constructive diffraction from crystal planes of spacing d.
A periodic structure of many parallel lines or planes that splits and diffracts a wave.
The smallest separation a probe can distinguish; a shorter wavelength gives a better resolution.
The idea that wave and particle descriptions are both needed yet never applied in the same measurement.
The value set by ℏ; classical physics is recovered when uncertainties become negligible compared with the system size.
Predicting a distribution of many measurement results rather than the trajectory of a single particle.
The average of many identical measurements of a quantity, obtained from the wavefunction.
A state of definite energy; the wavefunction is a solution of the time-independent Schrodinger equation for that energy.
The lowest allowed energy of a confined particle; in a box it is h²/8mL², not zero.
The situation where more than one quantum state has the same energy.
The thickness a particle must cross in tunnelling; transmission falls exponentially with it.
The fraction of incident particles or waves that get through a barrier.
